subject: Cognitive Science
title: Vigilance and Watchkeeping
description: A quick, practical guide to Vigilance and Watchkeeping.

hook.text: Radar operators in WWII had to spot rare blips on a screen for hours. Most targets were missed after thirty minutes.

buildup.text: Norman Mackworth built the clock test: watch a pointer and press a button when it double-jumps.

discovery.text: Performance dropped sharply after 15 minutes. Sustained attention decays predictably over time.

twist.text: Rare targets are the hardest. The rarer the event, the faster vigilance falls.

climax.text: Modern TSA agents face the same problem. Finding a rare weapon in thousands of bags is vigilance at its limit.

punchline.text: Attention isn't made for marathons—it's a sprinter.

quiz.question: What happens to sustained attention over time?

details.summary: Watchkeeping tasks, from radar monitoring to quality control, require sustained vigilance over long periods. Research since World War II has shown that human detection rates drop predictably and that environmental factors like lighting, noise, and shift length dramatically affect performance.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding watchkeeping limitations has saved lives in aviation, military, and medical settings where missed signals can be fatal.
takeaways: Human detection rates drop predictably over long watches
Environmental factors significantly affect vigilance performance
World War II radar monitoring research launched this field

faq.question: How did World War II contribute to vigilance research?
faq.answer: British radar operators frequently missed submarine signals during long watches. Norman Mackworth investigated and documented the vigilance decrement systematically, establishing the field of sustained attention research and influencing military watch schedules.

faq.question: What is the optimal watch duration for monitoring tasks?
faq.answer: Research suggests performance degrades significantly after 20 to 30 minutes. Many industries use two-hour maximum shifts with breaks for critical monitoring. Some high-stakes operations rotate watchers every 15 to 30 minutes to maintain detection rates.
